title: Trail mix
question: How do you pick trail mix?
decision: Trail mix of nuts and dried fruit, with little else listed.
why: Nuts and dried fruit are the old trail recipe, and the list runs in order of amount.
short_answer: Trail mix began as nuts and dried fruit carried on the trail. Ingredients run in order of amount, so the list shows what leads and what was added.
detail: Under 21 CFR 101.4, ingredients are listed in descending order of predominance. An extension guide makes the same point: the foods at the start of the list are the most in the recipe. Raw versus roasted nuts is its own question, with its own card. So is dried fruit.
kristy_take: In 1833, Danish students ate studenterhavre, “student oats”: raisins and almonds, with chocolate at the holidays. A 1906 camping guide sent hikers out with nuts, raisins and sweet chocolate. A 1958 novel packs raisins, peanuts, dried apricots and prunes.
cart_pick: Nuts and dried fruit, little else
buying_tips: Read the first few ingredients; nuts and fruit should lead.
Compare mixes by how short the list runs beyond nuts and fruit.
watch_out: A long list can push the nuts and fruit behind other ingredients.

labels_decoded.meaning: Listed in descending order of predominance, so the first one is the most.
An old word for trail mix; “good ol’ raisins and peanuts” is a backronym, and a 1913 dictionary has “gorp” as a verb.

tier_note: Nuts and fruit were the whole recipe on the old trails.
asked_as: which trail mix should i buy
how do i pick a trail mix
_do_line: Read the ingredients for anything added beyond the nuts and fruit.
